name: Vertical stripes / monochrome elongation
lead: Vertical stripes and single-colour outfits are a common piece of style advice, based on the belief that they make a person look taller and slimmer, while horizontal stripes make them look shorter and wider.[3] People use the approach to lengthen the visual line of the body: a vertical pattern or a head-to-toe monochrome outfit is meant to draw the eye up and down rather than across, so the figure reads as taller and leaner without any change to the body itself.

Researchers have examined the underlying visual illusion, and the results are mixed. A 2011 study in i-Perception reported that a square of horizontal lines looked taller and narrower than the same square drawn with vertical lines, and titled its finding as horizontal stripes not making people look fatter.[1] A 2013 follow-up reported a similar result for filled squares and found the effect varied between observers and with body build.[2]

A 2022 paper traced the common belief to a Japanese beauty handbook of 1813, showing the idea long predates modern fashion media.[3] No study specifically testing single-colour outfits for apparent height was found.

paras: Two related styling habits are grouped here. The first is wearing vertical stripes, pinstripes or other lines running from top to bottom. The second is monochrome or tonal dressing, in which top, trousers and often shoes are the same or similar colours, so the outfit forms one column instead of a series of colour breaks at the waist and hips. Stylists and fashion advice pieces commonly present both as ways to look taller and slimmer, and the idea is often applied to long jackets, high-rise trousers and matching footwear and trousers.

A 2022 study of an 1813 Japanese beauty handbook, Miyako Fuzoku Kewai Den, found the belief that striped clothing alters perceived body shape was already established over 200 years ago, when vertical striped patterns were popularised. The authors, Miyazaki and Ishibashi, argued that the belief was not born in modern times and that it persists among the public despite mixed empirical findings and the Helmholtz illusion pointing the other way.[3]
Monochrome dressing is described by proponents as creating one uninterrupted line, with fewer horizontal breaks to cut up the silhouette.

The vertical-horizontal illusion makes a vertical line look longer than a horizontal line of equal length, and the effect persists even when viewers know the lines are equal. Wikipedia reports that the inverted-T configuration produces the strongest effect and that urban and rural differences in susceptibility are inconsistent.[4] The Helmholtz illusion concerns filled versus unfilled space, and the original 19th-century claim was that a square divided by horizontal lines looks taller than one divided by vertical lines.[1]

Thompson and Mikellidou's 2011 paper in i-Perception applied this to fashion. They reported that a square of horizontal lines looks taller and narrower than an identical square of vertical lines: a vertical-striped rectangle had to be extended 7.1 percent vertically to match the height of a horizontal-striped square, and a horizontal-striped rectangle had to be 4.5 percent wider than a vertical-striped square to match its perceived width. The illusion held for a line drawing of a woman and for stereoscopically viewed photographs of a half-body mannequin, and a 3-D cylinder experiment found no support for horizontal lines being fattening; the authors concluded the evidence supported Helmholtz's original assertion.[1][5]

Ashida, Kuraguchi and Miyoshi's 2013 paper reported that a square with horizontal stripes looks thinner than one with vertical stripes, but identified three complications: the effect is stronger for thin figures and may reverse for fat ones; participants differ widely, suggesting dependence on which features they attend to; and the order in which fat and thin figures are shown produces strong hysteresis. They concluded the phenomenon is rather complex, and the paper's title says the illusion makes a person look fit only when they are already fit.[2][5]
These studies used abstract squares, line drawings and mannequins rather than people in everyday outfits, and no study specifically on monochrome outfits was found.

Descriptions of the practice in style guidance centre on matching colours from top to bottom, choosing fitted or high-waisted pieces so the line is not broken, and using pinstripe or vertical-pattern fabrics. The wiki does not rate these choices; the research summarised above concerns stripe orientation on shapes and figures rather than complete outfits.
No clinical studies found. Perception experiments on stripe orientation exist, summarised above.[1][2]

timeline.event: A Japanese beauty handbook, Miyako Fuzoku Kewai Den, records the belief that stripe direction affects perceived body shape.[3]
Thompson and Mikellidou publish a Helmholtz illusion study applied to fashion.[1]
Ashida, Kuraguchi and Miyoshi publish a follow-up on who the effect applies to.[2]
Miyazaki and Ishibashi publish their analysis of the 1813 handbook.[3]

lore.intro: Advice about stripes and tonal outfits circulates widely in style and fitness-adjacent spaces as a way to look taller or slimmer.

claims.claim: Vertical stripes make you look taller and slimmer.
claims.believers: This is a long-standing belief; a Japanese handbook from 1813 already recorded it when vertical stripes were popular.[3]
claims.experts: Perception studies using squares, drawings and mannequins reported the opposite direction for stripe orientation, with horizontal stripes looking taller and narrower, though individual results varied.[1][2]

claims.claim: Horizontal stripes make you look wider.
claims.believers: The common belief is that horizontal lines widen the figure.[3]
claims.experts: Thompson and Mikellidou's 2011 experiments found that horizontal lines made shapes look narrower, and the 2013 follow-up found the effect stronger for thin figures and possibly reversed for fat ones.[1][2]

claims.claim: Dressing in one colour makes you look taller.
claims.believers: Proponents describe the unbroken colour as creating one line from head to toe.
claims.experts: No published study was found testing single-colour outfits for apparent height or slimness.

card.summary: Dressing in vertical stripes or one colour to look taller and slimmer; the small perception literature points the other way for stripes.
card.note: Published stripe studies report horizontal stripes looking narrower, contrary to the common belief.

quick.overview:
The popular belief is that vertical stripes and head-to-toe single colours make a person look taller and slimmer.

Researchers have tested stripe direction in perception experiments. Two i-Perception studies reported horizontal stripes looking thinner, though the effect varied between viewers. No study on monochrome outfits was found.
quick.mechanism: The idea rests on optical illusions such as the vertical-horizontal and Helmholtz illusions, where line direction and filled space alter perceived length and width.

chain: Wear vertical stripes or one continuous colour
Eye follows an unbroken vertical line
Body looks longer and leaner in the observer's impression
angle.text: The practice changes how the outfit reads rather than the body. Wearers choose vertical lines, columns of one colour and tonal outfits hoping to look taller and slimmer; laboratory work on stripe direction has produced results that do not all point the way the belief predicts.
